newsitem.title: USA: House panel moves to build 9 more B-2 bombers.
newsitem.headline: House panel moves to build 9 more B-2 bombers.

text.p: A House panel called Thursday for spending more than $500 million to build nine stealth B-2 bombers that the Air Force says it does not need.
At the same time, the House National Security Committee, over strong Pentagon protests, slashed $800 million from the Navy's F/A-18 E/F Super Hornet aircraft budget request.
In its version of the fiscal 1998 defence authorisation bill, the panel authorised $503.3 million to re-establish parts of the B-2 production line that have been shut down.

It said these funds, $331.2 million more than President Clinton's request for the controversial bomber programme, should finance the procurement of nine bat-wing B-2s to supplement the currently planned 21-strong fleet.
"The committee believes that the current fleet ... is insufficient to meet the likely contingencies and crises of the next 30 to 40 years," the panel said in its report.

The full House may vote on the committee's recommendations -- adopted by a lopsided 51-to-3 vote Wednesday night -- as early as next week. The Senate Armed Service Committee was marking up its own version of the bill behind closed doors Thursday. A conference committee would iron out differences.
Northrop Grumman Corp., prime contractor for the B-2, has delivered 13 B-2s to the Air Force so far, with the final eight to be handed over by the end of next year.
The Pentagon has opposed expanding the fleet beyond 21, preferring instead to pursue less costly ways of meeting potential threats.
But with several thousand subcontractors spread around the country eager for additional sales, political pressure to order more bombers has come from congressional Republicans and Democrats alike.
Captain Leo Devine, an Air Force spokesman, declined comment on the panel's action but said: "As far as the Air Force is concerned, 21's our number," referring to the B-2 fleet.

In slashing funds for the Super Hornet, the committee said it strongly supported modernisation of the rapidly ageing tactical aircraft fleet, but termed the long-term costs of the Pentagon's plan "staggering."

Defence Secretary William Cohen, in a letter to panel members late Tuesday night, said it was "urgent" to restore full funding of the Navy's $2.1 billion request for 20 Super Hornets in fiscal 1998, which begins Oct. 1.
But the committee recommended $1.3 billion, said by experts to be enough to procure perhaps only 7 to 10 of the aircraft to continue operational evaluation.
In another setback for the Pentagon, the panel called for earmarking $153.3 million for research and development of the F/A-18 E/F aircraft design, $114.2 million less than Clinton's request.
"Without the F/A-18 E/F we would be sending our pilots into combat at the turn of the century with the 1970s technology of the F/A-18 C/D," Cohen wrote.
He said the 20 F/A-18 E/Fs sought by Clinton were needed to deploy with battle groups in 2001, 10 years before the earliest projected fleet debut of the multiservice Joint Strike Fighter.
A Pentagon spokesman, Captain Mike Doubleday, said Thursday that the Defence Department was "heartened" that the panel had provided at least some funding for the Super Hornet programme.
